title: Misinformation, believability, and vaccine acceptance over 40 countries: Takeaways from the initial phase of the COVID-19 infodemic
screen_reason: Global survey (18,314 respondents, 40 countries, June-July 2020) that asked respondents whether they had seen or heard each of 11 fact-checked-false COVID-19 claims in the last month, and reports the weighted share of respondents exposed to each claim. That is a self-reported exposure share with a population denominator (RECALL). The believability and vaccine-acceptance analyses are belief/effects work and are excluded, but the descriptive exposure shares carry the paper into the review.

estimates.country: 40 countries (all continents; countries shown in Fig 1)
estimates.platform: Online survey recruited via the Facebook Advertising Platform; the exposure question is not platform-specific ('seen or heard')
estimates.date: 18 June to 13 July 2020 (English 18-25 June; Portuguese, Spanish, French 22-28 June; Arabic and top-up 7-13 July)
estimates.measure_type: % of survey respondents who report having seen or heard the false claim 'Drugs' in the last month
estimates.value_raw: Drugs: 84.2% of respondents (weighted average across 40 countries)
estimates.denominator: 18,314 complete survey responses from adults (18+) in 40 countries, recruited through Facebook advertisements and post-stratified by raking on age, sex and country
estimates.definition: Respondent answered the exposure item 'Have you seen or heard this information in the last month?' (options: Yes, Partly, No, I don't remember) for the claim: Existing drugs for malaria and HIV can help treat COVID-19
estimates.misinfo_def: “Corroborating these claims with fact-checked information from credible sources, including the World Health Organization (WHO)’s Mythbusters and the International Fact-Checking Network (IFCN)’s #CoronaVirusFacts Alliance database, we arrived at the following list of 11 false claims”
estimates.source_quote: Drugs and Weather are the two most popular claims, with an average of 84.2% and 77.1% of participants encountering these rumors, respectively.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Exposure is measured by asking respondents whether they had encountered the claim, so the estimate itself is SELF-REPORT (corrected from 'fact_checker', which described the provenance of the claim set rather than of the measurement). The claims put to respondents were independently established as false by fact-checkers, as recorded here: Falsity of each claim was established by the authors before fielding: over 200 COVID-19 rumours were collected from DXY.cn (18 March 2020), reduced to 30 health-behaviour pieces and combined into 11 distinct claims, each corroborated against WHO Mythbusters and the IFCN #CoronaVirusFacts Alliance database. Exposure itself is respondent self-report (‘Have you seen or heard this information in the last month?’); the paper does not state how the 'Yes' and 'Partly' options were combined into the reported percentage.
estimates.moderator_quote: Our final dataset consisted of 805,816 complete responses (N = 18,314) from 40 countries (see Fig 1). Our sample covers all continents and contains a median of 464 respondents per country.
estimates.notes: Weighted (raking to UN 2019 World Population Prospects age/sex distributions) average across the 40 countries. One of eleven claim-level exposure estimates from the SAME survey sample; the paper reports no aggregate 'exposed to any rumour' figure. Highest-exposure claim in the study; the Discussion loosely restates Drugs and Weather as reaching 'nearly three-fourths of all respondents globally', which understates the 84.2%/77.1% figures.

missed_or_uncertain: 1) POOLING WARNING for the adjudicator: the ten rows above are ten claim-level exposure estimates from ONE survey sample (N=18,314). The paper reports no 'exposed to at least one rumour' aggregate, so there is no single poolable headline number; if the review pools one row per study, these should be collapsed (Drugs, at 84.2%, is the highest and Dryer, at 27.4%, the lowest). 2) Gargling ('Gargling with salt water can prevent coronavirus infection') is the eleventh claim but no global weighted average is stated. Only hedged country statements are given: 'widely disseminated in Saudi Arabia, Iraq, and Nicaragua (i.e., above 90%), with markedly low exposure in the UK, Spain and Sweden (i.e., 40% or less)' and 'nearly 90% of respondents from Saudi Arabia and Iraq reported to have seen the claim compared to only around 20% of respondents in Sweden and Finland'. These are thresholds and approximations, not verbatim point estimates with denominators, so no country rows were created (R8). Country-level values exist in Fig 3, Fig 4 and S1 Fig but are not readable as numbers in the text. 3) BELIEF, excluded by protocol: 'On average, we observe that 22% of respondents per country are predisposed to believing in rumors', highest 'more than 31%' in Yemen, Algeria, Saudi Arabia and Tunisia, lowest 'a mere 7.4%' in Sweden and Finland. Believability is belief/susceptibility, not exposure. 4) FACT-CHECK EXPOSURE, not misinformation exposure: 48.6% of participants saw a fact-check on the Drugs rumour and 40.3% on Weather; all other fact-checks were seen by no more than 25%. Not extracted since the numerator is accurate content. 5) Sample-size discrepancy in the paper: the Abstract says 'over 18,400 individuals', the Discussion says '18,407 complete responses', and the Methods final dataset is 'N = 18,314'. The Methods figure is used. 6) The paper does not state whether the exposure percentage counts only 'Yes' or 'Yes' plus 'Partly'; the authors themselves flag that 'mere exposure to debunking information from a news agency might be construed as exposure to misinformation'.

rob.design: Non-probability online survey recruited through Facebook advertisements (independent campaigns per country, four age-group ad sets: 18-24, 25-44, 45-64, 65+), fielded 18 June to 13 July 2020 in English, French, Spanish, Portuguese and Arabic. 1,946,516 ad responses / N=44,239 clicked through; after dropping incomplete responses, duplicated IP addresses, respondents who withheld sex, and countries with fewer than 30 complete responses, the analytic sample was 805,816 item responses (N=18,314 respondents) from 40 countries, median 464 respondents per country. Post-stratification by raking on age and sex against UN 2019 World Population Prospects. No response rate can be computed for an advertisement-recruited sample. Exposure is self-reported for 11 pre-selected claims verified as false against WHO Mythbusters and the IFCN #CoronaVirusFacts database; no intercoder reliability applies. Authors state results 'are not strictly representative of the world population', over-sample economically undeveloped countries, and omit Chinese, Indic and Slavic languages.
rob.item6_quote: Corroborating these claims with fact-checked information from credible sources, including the World Health Organization (WHO)’s Mythbusters [23] and the International Fact-Checking Network (IFCN)’s #CoronaVirusFacts Alliance database [24], we arrived at the following list of 11 false claims
rob.item10_quote: When we examine the overall exposure, we note that some claims have exceptionally high public appeal. Drugs and Weather are the two most popular claims, with an average of 84.2% and 77.1% of participants encountering these rumors, respectively. Vaccination-related claims show moderate-to-high exposure with Tracking being seen by 60.7%, Population by 57.6% and Pharma by 55.7% of the respondents. A smaller portion of respondents were exposed to do-it-yourself (DIY) rumors on preventive measures with Sunbath seen by 54.7%, Water by 44.3%, Vinegar by 34.9%, and Dryer by 27.4% of the respondents.
